projects.title: The Treasure Within
projects.contextText: This project was developed for the Multimedia Communication course, part of my Design & Multimedia degree at the University of Coimbra.
projects.description: An immersive 3D web experience inspired by Disney's Treasure Planet. You pilot a voxel galleon through space toward planets that embody human emotions: Happiness, Courage, Love and Hope. The real treasure is internal, not gold.
body: Developed in the 3rd year, for the Multimedia Communication course, with Daniel Costa, the project reinterprets the Disney film around personal growth. Daniel produced the base 3D assets while I led the development: Three.js programming, sensor integration, performance optimisation, rigging and sound engineering.

To hold a fluid 60 FPS in the browser I followed a strict technical pipeline. Models started as voxels in MagicaVoxel, passed through Blender for geometry cleanup and polygon reduction, and characters were rigged in Mixamo before everything was exported as .GLB. A global LoadingManager pre-loads every 3D and audio file into memory before the experience starts. I replaced heavy opacity maths with native Additive Blending for the planets' holographic glow, and simulated the universe with a skydome whose dynamic colour filters shift the lighting according to the visitor's real local hour.

The core of the code dropped menus and read the real world instead. I wired the Web Audio API to the microphone so the player must raise their voice on the Planet of Courage, used MediaPipe to read the camera and confirm a smile on the Planet of Happiness, built a rhythm mini-game with anti-cheat cooldowns on the Planet of Love, and a glitch simulation on Hope that tests the visitor's patience. The journey closes on a PHP/JSON backend where travellers leave reflections for others. An exhausting project, and one awarded top marks.

chapters.title: Concept and vision
body: The starting point was Disney's Treasure Planet (2002), a film where a nineteenth-century sailing galleon crosses space looking for Captain Flint's treasure. Watching it again, we realised the gold is the least interesting part of it.

The film is about Jim Hawkins growing up, finding his confidence, and finding a father figure where he was not expecting one. That reading is the one we took all the way: here the treasure is internal.
We built the Etherium, a sea of stars with four planets, and every planet is an emotion: Courage, Happiness, Love and Hope. The visitor does not watch a Captain on screen, the visitor is the Captain.
The sky follows your computer's local clock, so whoever arrives at three in the morning does not see the same Etherium as someone arriving at midday.
chapters.sub: Reinterpreting Sci-Fi Nostalgia

chapters.title: Voxel and Cyber-Sailpunk
body: We modelled the whole world in blocks, in MagicaVoxel. It reads well at any distance: a planet two hundred units away still has a silhouette, and a cube costs the GPU almost nothing.

On top of that we put a green-phosphor CRT terminal. We called it cyber-sailpunk: nineteenth-century wood, rigging and sails living beside computer interfaces and thrusters. It is the film's own logic, moved over to the software side.

The same block was the rule for everything. Ship, crew and planets came off the same grid, and the planets had to be taken apart into separate meshes in Blender so the rings and satellites could turn on their own.

The crew alternates between idle and walking, and each one carries a hitbox so it cannot walk through the hull. Morph is the exception: no skeleton at all, animated in code with sines and cosines, which for a blob of jelly worked better than any rig.
chapters.question: Why voxel and cyber-sailpunk?

chapters.title: No Ball Leaves in a Straight Line
body: Each cannonball starts with an initial velocity and is then under a constant downward acceleration, which traces an arc. Since there is no ground in the Etherium, the ball never hits anything: it keeps falling and drifts away until it is gone.

We kept the endless fall because it sells the scale of the void better than any explosion would. Attached to every ball is a trail that dissipates behind it, and that is what keeps the trajectory readable once the ball is far away.

The thrusters follow the same logic: the count and size of the particles scale with the ship's speed, so when you accelerate you see the engine pulling. The sound follows, rising and falling with acceleration, and you hear your speed before you look at the screen.
chapters.sub: Ballistics, trails and thrusters

chapters.title: A Terminal That Notices You
body: There are no menus anywhere. The opening terminal shrinks when the game starts and goes to live in a corner of the screen. It is the one that asks your name and uses it from then on: everything that in another game would be a pause panel is here the terminal talking to you.

The tutorial lives in the same place and is implicit. The game blocks until you press W and fire the thrusters, and only then asks you to fire the cannons. There is no instructions screen: you learn to move by moving.

It is also the terminal that writes the Captain's Log while you play. By the end of a session there is a document that did not exist before, different from anybody else's, and you take it with you. It is the only part of the Etherium that still exists after you close the tab.

Since visitors write into the Log and leave messages on the Mural dos Viajantes, the travellers' wall, that text is treated as untrusted: it goes through an escapeHTML() before it reaches the DOM, with a banned word filter on top. It is dull work, but the moment someone can write onto another person's screen it stops being optional.
chapters.question: How do you teach someone to play with no menus at all?

video.alt: The opening terminal, in green phosphor, writing the boot diagnostic and asking for the Captain's name before it hands over the controls.

chapters.title: Four Emotions, Four Input Channels
body: Every planet is an emotion and every emotion has a mechanic of its own. The ambition was to use every input channel the browser gives us, the microphone, the camera, the timing between keypresses and the complete absence of action, so the code reads the real world instead of counting clicks. A click is always the same click. A shout is not.

In Courage, the microphone feeds a Web Audio API analyser reading volume in real time, and you have to hold three seconds above the threshold. Courage is rarely about swords, it is about having the strength to break the silence, and if you play in silence you do not get past this.

In Happiness we open the camera and run MediaPipe's FaceLandmarker, looking for a smile. In Love you hear a heartbeat and have to press in time with it: if you mash the key, your progress goes backwards, because love needs time and needs you to align with someone else's rhythm.

The last one is Hope, and it is doing nothing. The terminal starts glitching and looks like it has crashed, and the only way through is to press nothing at all and wait for it to stabilise on its own. It works against instinct, because when a screen fails the normal reaction is to hit every key.

start.alt: Two voxel planets, Hope in green and Happiness in gold, each with its own ring of blocks.

end.alt: Two voxel planets, Courage in blue and Love in pink with a heart cut into its surface.

video.alt: The four planets, each unlocked by a different sensor: shouting into the microphone, smiling at the camera, pressing in time with a heartbeat, and waiting.

chapters.title: The Players Who Froze and the Planet That Crashed
body: In the user tests, people entered the game and simply stood still looking at the ship. We had built a world with total freedom of flight and nobody realised they could fly. That is where the decision came from: let the terminal teach, instead of having instructions.

Then came the opposite problem. With total freedom, players flew off into the void and got lost, with no reference to come back to. The terminal learned to notice you had left the route and to offer to recalculate, with a sonar sound pointing the way. It stays an offer, not a forced correction.

On the model side, the MagicaVoxel exports carried thousands of hidden vertices nobody could see in the viewer. The first planet we put into the code brought the game down, and every model had to be cleaned by hand in Blender, one at a time.

Rigging in Mixamo was another nightmare: rubber skeletons, Silver's arm bending the wrong way, Jim simply refusing the rig. And we asked AIs for help with the collision and camera maths, which broke the code further and left the ship flying upside down. The hard part we had to work out on paper.

slot.what: A paper sketch, exactly as it is. Ugly is the evidence.

chapters.title: This Runs on a Phone
body: This runs on a phone, and it is not a cut-down version. It was a challenge we set ourselves at the start: the same experience, whole, in portrait and in landscape, so the project had to solve two formats instead of one.

The four mechanics did not change. The shout, the smile, the heartbeat and the wait work in exactly the same way, because a phone's microphone and camera are the same sensors the browser was already using.

What changed is what you cannot see. The particles were reduced, and the sky, which turns constantly on a desktop, only turns on a phone while the ship is stopped. There is no sense spending processing on movement nobody notices while they are sailing.
The controls are the one thing designed from scratch. A round pad to steer the ship, and a firing button that appears when there is something to fire at.
chapters.sub: Portrait and landscape, and the same four mechanics

depth.alt: An iPhone resting on a mound of moss against black, the game's green-phosphor terminal writing an entry in the Captain's Log.

chapters.title: Who Did What
body: I, Rogério Correia, was the lead developer. I built the Three.js structure, the cameras, the lights, the game loop, the MediaPipe integration, the Web Audio API, the rhythm logic behind the Love mechanic and the project documentation. Daniel Costa modelled 3D assets in MagicaVoxel. From there the models were mine to finish: the cleanup in Blender, the rigging and the animation through Mixamo, the scenery built around them, and most of the concept the game rests on.

The split was not neutral and it was not drawn from a hat. We chose it because one member of the team was less comfortable with programming, and giving him a defined piece of the modelling was how both of us could produce usable work inside the deadline. Saying it plainly is more honest than pretending it was an even division of tasks.

projects.title: The Veldt
projects.contextText: This project was developed for the Project 3 course, part of my Design & Multimedia degree at the University of Coimbra.
projects.description: Inspired by Ray Bradbury's short story, The Veldt is an interactive 3D website that takes the visitor inside the Nursery, a virtual simulation room where an African savanna comes to life. The project carries the idea of a physical pop-up book into the browser, letting you explore the space in first person and piece the story together in any order through interactive points of interest.
body: Developed in the Project 3 course (3rd year) with Afonso Almeida and Tiago Gomes, the experience grew directly out of a printed editorial object: the goal was to give that physical piece a third dimension by placing the visitor inside the scene. On the team I led the Three.js implementation, modelled most of the environments in Blender, tuned the animations through rigging, and handled performance.

The art direction blends the retro aesthetic of 1950s computers (the era the story was written) with the savanna simulation. To reinforce the idea that the room is a 'fake' technological illusion, I used a visual trick: only nearby elements are modelled in low-poly 3D, while the horizon and distant elements are flat 2D images. Combined with Three.js instancing, this kept the project extremely light, running well on both desktop and mobile.

I modelled the environments with shade-smooth lighting and animated everything from scratch with skeletons: the lions, the vultures, the intro sequence. Collisions use invisible cylindrical and spherical hitboxes at the bases of trees and rocks, with boolean debug flags to visualise and fine-tune each blocking zone. For sound I did dense work in ElevenLabs to design the characters' voices; audio and text are triggered by the camera's (X, Y, Z) position relative to trigger zones, computing distance and volume to build a spatial, immersive soundscape.

chapters.title: Stepping into the story
chapters.sub: With a technology none of us had used before
body: The Veldt was made for the Project 3 course and is based on Ray Bradbury's short story of the same name. In the story, a family lives in an automated house with a special room, the Nursery, that projects whatever the children imagine onto its walls. In this case, an African savanna full of lions.

The goal was to turn the story into an interactive multimedia piece that worked in the browser. We wanted visitors to do more than read the story. We wanted them inside the Nursery, exploring it in first person.

The hardest part was the technology. None of us had worked with Three.js before, so we spent a lot of time researching how to use it well without making it too heavy. We also had to think from the start about whether it would run on a phone.

video.alt: The start screen, START SIMULATION, giving way to the savannah of the nursery: orange sand, acacia trees and a hard blue sky.

chapters.title: A story in any order
chapters.sub: Every object holds a piece of the story
body: Instead of telling the story from start to finish, we spread it around the room. There are no goals and no arrows showing the way. Whoever walks in decides where to go.

There are six points of interest taken from the story: the lions, the vulture, the deer, George's wallet, Lydia's scarf and the Nursery door. When you get close to one and interact with it, an excerpt from the book appears on screen and is read out loud. Because there is no set order, each person puts the story together in their own way.

The interface is inspired by 1950s computers, the decade the story was written in, with a simple grid and the JetBrains Mono typeface. The warm colours come from the savanna, and the light never changes, as a reminder that the landscape is not real.

A vulture alone against the blue sky, with the prompt to analyse it in the middle of the screen.
Lydia's scarf on the ground under a tree, dark blue with red on it.
George's wallet left in the grass beside two rocks, small enough to walk straight past.
A door standing on its own in the middle of the sand, closed, with its shadow next to it.

chapters.title: How we built the room
chapters.sub: Close up it's 3D, far away it's a picture
body: The models were made in Blender, low poly with shade smooth, and the textures were prepared in Photoshop. To keep it light in the browser and on phones, we only modelled in 3D what sits close to the visitor. The horizon and anything far away are flat images.

The animations were made in Blender with bones, which made it much easier to bring them into Three.js. The lions and the vulture loop, and right after you enter, Lydia's scarf moves to catch your eye and pull you closer. To stop people walking through trees or off the map, we added invisible hitboxes to the trees, the rocks and the edges of the room.

The voices of George, Lydia and the narrator were generated in ElevenLabs, with emotion cues for each line. The ambient sounds come from Freesound and were edited to match the animations. When a narration starts, the background sound drops so the voice is easy to hear.
On a computer you walk with the keyboard and look around with the mouse. On a phone there is an on-screen joystick, and the experience asks you to turn the phone sideways.

video.alt: The scene turning in Blender: the low poly rocks, trees and grass in front, and behind them the flat painted planes that make the horizon.

chapters.title: The final test
chapters.sub: One QR code and the whole room exploring
body: At the final presentation we showed a QR code, and people in the room, teachers included, tried it straight away on their phones. It went really well and turned into a fun moment for everyone.
The project is still online and can be explored on a computer or a phone. Headphones are recommended.

projects.title: Soft Capture
projects.contextText: This project was developed for the Project 4 course, part of my Design & Multimedia degree at the University of Coimbra.
projects.description: Soft Capture is an interactive installation and social experiment made for the FeedNPlay at the University of Coimbra's DEI, a wall of 9 screens at 7000×1080 pixels. It explores biometric surveillance, digital consent and algorithmic bias. A camera captures whoever walks up and an AI builds a 3D avatar with an invented social and psychological profile. When the person tries to delete that data, they find out they can't.
body: Developed in the Interactive Multimedia IV course (Project 4, 3rd year) with Carolina Seixas and Maria Alice Neves, the project starts from how easily we hand over our data. I covered the whole technical and interface side: the Three.js and JavaScript architecture, 3D modelling, UI/UX design in Figma, WebGL animation and ecosystem integration.

Moving a 3D application onto a 9-screen wall (7000×1080px) took a lot of on-site testing. The orthographic camera in Three.js, the viewing angles and the projection ratios all had to be calibrated so the avatars and interface would not distort across the monitor seams. In Blender we modelled the avatars' modular parts (hair, glasses, body types) and built a code pipeline that assembles the character in real time via GLTFLoader and SkeletonUtils, from the JSON returned by the Gemini 2.5-Flash API.

Navigation is fully contactless. I used the camera and MediaPipe Holistic to map the visitor's hand as a cursor on a canvas, triggering capture when the hand rises above the head, plus microphone clap-detection to re-sort the avatars by inferred category. Body animation reacts to the AI-assigned psychological traits, and to hold a stable 60 FPS I capped the canvas at 30 simultaneous avatars, archiving older profiles through a PHP/JSON server.

chapters.title: A wall of 9 screens
chapters.sub: And no mouse or keyboard in sight
body: Soft Capture was the group project for the Project 4 course. The brief asked for an interactive multimedia piece built around a current theme, designed to be used without a mouse or keyboard.

It was made for the FeedNPlay at DEI, a wall of 9 screens at 7000 by 1080 pixels. That brought a challenge of its own, because almost nothing that works on a normal screen works on a wall that wide, seen from a distance.

chapters.title: What the machine thinks you are
chapters.sub: One photo is enough to judge you
body: We started from how easily we hand over our data. We wanted to show how someone's appearance can be turned into a profile and a judgement, and how hard it is to go back once you agree to join a system.

The installation captures whoever walks up and uses an AI to build an avatar with a profile. Besides visible details, like hair colour or clothes, the profile includes guesses about their job, social class, income or political views. They are made up, and that is exactly what exposes the bias these systems carry.
All the avatars live in the same world, in full view of anyone passing by. Some of our references were the Nintendo Wii Miis, The Sims, Black Mirror and Take This Lollipop.

sources.alt: The avatar alone on a white screen under the word INSPECTION, waiting to be read.
The full read-out for one avatar. Height, weight and hair on the left; on the right a profession, a social class, an income and a politics, each with a confidence percentage printed under it.

chapters.title: How you get into the system
chapters.sub: Raising your hand means saying yes
body: When nobody is in front of the wall, the avatars wander around the world and a message invites people to take part. Whoever walks up is picked up by the camera and asked to raise a hand above their head for two seconds. When the time is up, a photo is taken.

The photo is analysed in three steps: first the physical appearance, then an invented profile and, finally, a few details that depend on gender. With that data, the avatar is dressed with the person's clothes, colours and hair, and gets a way of walking that matches the personality the AI gave it.

Before the new avatar arrives, all the others look up. Then it drops from the sky and joins the crowd. From there, the hand works as a cursor: hold it over an avatar to open its profile, wave to close it, and clap to group everyone by themes like politics, social class or mood.

chapters.title: The button that doesn't delete
chapters.sub: You gave consent, your data is ours
body: Every profile has a button to delete the avatar. When the hand moves over it, the progress ring never fills up and a message appears instead: "You gave consent, your data is ours."

This is where the idea behind the project becomes clearest. The person agreed to take part with a gesture and, when they want to take it back, they can't. Even behind the scenes nothing disappears. The world shows the 30 most recent avatars, and older ones are moved to a history file instead of being deleted.

chapters.title: Taking it all to the wall
chapters.sub: At 7000 pixels wide, nothing is simple
body: The avatars were modelled in Blender from two bases, one male and one female, with clothing pieces and skin and hair textures adjusted to look natural. The walking and idle animations come from Mixamo and change with the personality. In code, each avatar is cloned and dressed in real time from the AI's data.

For the analysis we started with a model running locally through Ollama and later moved to Gemini. Each photo triggers three requests, and the invented profile is always treated as fiction, never as a real assessment of the person.

The hardest part was the wall itself. At 7000 pixels wide, the Three.js orthographic camera, the area the avatars can walk in and the size of the text all had to be worked out from the screen's dimensions, and the profile panel was redesigned so it would not get lost in the middle of the image. This only makes sense when you test it on site, so I spent a lot of time at the FeedNPlay.

The gestures took even more work. The distance to the wall, the depth of the room and the lighting made detection unstable. I ended up replacing the HandLandmarker, which was heavy and barely detected anything, with the wrists from MediaPipe's PoseLandmarker, and smoothed the cursor with a filter and a dead zone, because on a wall that size a small tremble of the hand becomes a huge jump. The cursor always follows the hand raised highest.

chapters.title: A world full of avatars
chapters.sub: Even the teachers wanted in
body: For the final presentation, Soft Capture was set up on the FeedNPlay. There were some really funny moments, with people creating their avatar, discovering the profile the AI made up for them and exploring everyone else's. The teachers wanted to create theirs too and really enjoyed it.
The project is online and can be opened in the browser, but it was made for that wall, and that is where it makes the most sense.

projects.title: Modular City
projects.contextText: This project was developed for the Computer Graphics course, part of my Design & Multimedia degree at the University of Coimbra.
projects.description: Modular City is a computer graphics and generative architecture study built in Processing. It is a 3D simulation of a city inspired by New York, with housing blocks, a central park and a lake, where the heights, the facades and the roofs are generated again, differently, every time it runs.
body: Built solo in the Computer Graphics course (2nd year), the work focused on generation algorithms, spatial maths and real-time rendering optimisation. The scene was conceived from scratch to be robust and interactive, meant to be embedded on the web as a portfolio centrepiece.

The core is a 20×20 grid read from numeric files, where each value sets the ground type (road, building, park or water). Generative maths decides building heights under a rule-tuned probability distribution, deliberately fighting the natural tendency toward repetitive average values to force visually dynamic skylines. Conditional rules assign UV textures (hand-made in Photoshop) and distinct roof shapes according to height.

For the lake I split the water cells in two to densify the mesh and joined the intermediate vertices with an oscillating equation combined with Perlin Noise for realistic ripples. I worked around Processing's native limit on active lights by using emission materials to fake light points, and modelled street lamps on the grid to which the algorithm randomly assigns real lights on each generation. The scene is completed by a plane flying over, with vector translation maths, bank turns and collision avoidance.

chapters.title: A city made only of code
chapters.sub: No models, just vertices
body: Modular City was the solo project for the Computer Graphics course, in my second year. The brief was simple: build a city in Processing with at least three kinds of object and one composite object.

The main rule was that nothing could come from a modelling program. Every object had to be built from vertices, in code, and the city had to move: something travelling and something turning. A second stage added textures, two light sources and materials with real shine.

media.alt: The whole city from above, on black: the blocks in their grid, and the plane crossing over them.

chapters.title: A grid that never comes out the same
chapters.sub: The city changes every time it starts
body: The city is read from a text file holding a 19 by 19 grid. Each number says what sits in that cell: road, building, park or water. The plan is always the same, built on the straight streets of New York, but the city that grows from it never is.

Every time the program starts, each building gets a new height between 70 and 180. That height decides the rest: the facade texture and the roof type come from rules tied to it, with some combinations kept for the tallest buildings. The skyline comes out different on every run without ever stopping looking like the same city.

chapters.title: Building it all by hand
chapters.sub: From a cube to a plane, point by point
body: Every solid is built by hand, point by point: cube, prism, pyramid, trapezium, cylinder, cone and sphere, each one also in a version ready to take a texture. The whole city is made of those pieces.
The building and roof textures were made by me in Photoshop, often by mixing several illustrations together until the facade held up at the distance it is seen from.

The lake does not use the city grid. It is a mesh of its own, 40 by 40 and far denser, where every vertex rises and falls with Perlin noise. The edges stay fixed, otherwise the water would come away from the ground.

The plane was the hardest part. Besides being modelled piece by piece, it flies on vectors: it points where it is going, banks into the turn, straightens up slowly and reverses when it reaches the edge of the map. I ended up making sketches in a notebook to work out how the pieces sat against each other in space. There is also a boat on the lake, moving the same way.

sources.alt: The first notebook page, in pencil: the plane roughed out as a set of boxes, with the coordinate axes drawn beside it.
The page after it: the same shapes with every corner given a letter, which is how each vertex got its coordinates in the code.

chapters.title: When the city goes dark
chapters.sub: Only seven real lights
body: The city has a day and a night. At night the general light drops and the street lamps take over, modelled into the grid next to the buildings.

Processing will not hold many real lights at once, so only seven lamps truly light up. They are drawn at random, but from a fixed seed, so it is always the same ones and they never jump from one place to another. The rest are faked with an emissive material, which glows without lighting anything around it.
There are also lights that blink on their own on top of some buildings and on the plane's wing, on random intervals.

video.alt: The city going from day to night: the sky darkens, the street lamps come on and the lights start blinking on the towers and on the plane's wing.

chapters.title: More than the brief asked for
chapters.sub: And then it ended up in the browser
body: The teacher really liked it and it was one of the best marks I have had. What surprised him was the technical side: the waves on the lake, the way the plane moves and how it was modelled.
I built a fair amount the brief never asked for, like the night mode, the boat, the street lamps and an export of the city to a 3D file, plus a capture that circles the whole city.
Later I wanted the city to run in a browser and, since Processing does not go to the web, the code was rebuilt in p5.js. That is the version you can see here.

media.alt: Closer in: the central park with its trees, the lake with the boat on it, and the buildings of every height around them.

projects.title: Audácia
projects.contextText: This project was developed for the Typography in Digital Media course, part of my Design & Multimedia degree at the University of Coimbra.
projects.description: An interactive poster built around the word Audácia, audacity. The word is on fire, and the fire grows as whoever is watching walks towards the screen.

chapters.title: A word I did not choose
chapters.sub: Only type, and it had to react
body: The brief handed every student in the class a different word, and mine was Audácia. Audacity. The job was to turn it into a poster for a large screen in a public space, in portrait, and to make that poster react to whoever walked past it.

Two rules shaped everything after that. The poster could use typography and lettering and nothing else, so no photographs and no illustration. And the interaction had to be built on the viewer's position, proximity or movement, because those are the only things the screen wall it was designed for can read.

chapters.title: Come closer and it burns
chapters.sub: Distance is the whole interaction
body: Audacity is the nerve to face something you would rather avoid, so I made the word itself the thing to be faced. It sits on black, small and almost cold, and it burns more the nearer you get.

Standing back is safe and the fire dies down to almost nothing. Walking up to the screen makes the word grow and catch, until it fills the frame and is hard to look at straight. You have to actually commit and take the steps, which means the interaction is not decoration on top of the word. It is the word being acted out.

chapters.title: Two answers instead of one
chapters.sub: The fire in one program, the life in another
body: The brief let us choose: either a video simulation made in motion graphics software, or a working prototype written in code. I did not want to pick, because each one was missing what the other had, so I made both and joined them.

The fire was animated in After Effects, where the word could be given the quality it needed, and then exported one frame at a time. Six hundred and four images went into the sketch's data folder, from the word barely glowing to the word fully alight.

Processing plays that sequence, but never in order. OpenCV finds the face in the camera with a frontal cascade, and the width of the box it draws around it, somewhere between 50 and 300 pixels, is mapped straight onto the frame number. Distance does not set a speed, it sets which frame is on screen, so walking forward runs the animation on and stepping back winds it in.

Face detection is never perfectly steady, and a frame number that followed it exactly would jump around and look broken. So the frame being shown chases the one it should be on rather than snapping to it, closing five percent of the gap every time the screen is redrawn. That small delay is what makes the fire look like it is breathing instead of shaking.

While I was testing, the camera image and the green detection box were drawn on screen so I could see what the algorithm was reading. The poster itself shows only the word. The camera reads, it never appears.

chapters.title: Doing both was the answer
chapters.sub: Original, and it actually ran
body: It was well received. The teachers marked it well, and what they picked out was that the idea was original and that it worked, which for an interactive poster are two different things and both had to be true.

The part that made the difference was refusing to choose between the two options. Handing in only the video would have looked right and done nothing. Handing in only the code would have done something and looked rough. Putting the After Effects animation inside the Processing sketch gave the poster the finish of one and the behaviour of the other.
It stayed a prototype, presented in class in two minutes. It was made for the screen wall in the department, but it never ran there.

projects.title: Quebra Jazz Identity
projects.partners: Afonso Almeida · Laura Freire · Tiago Gomes
projects.contextText: This project was developed for the Web Identity course, part of my Design & Multimedia degree at the University of Coimbra.
projects.description: A rebrand for Quebra Jazz, the free open air festival on the Quebra-Costas steps in Coimbra. The mark came out of a satellite photograph of the staircase, which looks like a saxophone from above.

mockups.alt: QUEBRA JAZZ set in a fractured typeface, its letters broken into fragments
mockups.caption: Wordmark

chapters.title: A festival that already exists
chapters.sub: We took a real one instead of inventing one
body: The brief was a complete visual identity for a fictional client, chosen from three options. We took the music festival, and then did not invent one.

Quebra Jazz is real. It is a free open air jazz festival held on the Quebra-Costas steps, in the old town of Coimbra, which is the city we study in. It runs on the idea that culture should not be paid for at the door, it puts emerging musicians on the same programme as established ones, and it happens on a staircase people walk up every day.
Choosing something real meant we could not decide what the brand stood for. It already stood for something and our job was to find out what, and then look at it.

chapters.title: The first idea was a cliché
chapters.sub: And we were the ones who said so
body: The first route was a typeface built out of musical instruments, saxophones and flutes worked into the letterforms. The second was breaking the words apart, playing with type and fragments to say the word quebra, which means break.

Both were dropped, and the reason is written in our own document at the time. The instruments were the obvious answer, the thing anybody designing for jazz reaches for first. The fragments made compositions that were interesting to look at and impossible to read quickly or remember afterwards, which are the two things a mark has to do. Neither had the sophistication we had put at the centre of the brief.
We wrote that down and started again. Losing three weeks to an idea is cheaper than carrying a bad one to the end because it was the first one.

chapters.title: The staircase, seen from a satellite
chapters.sub: From above, it looks like a saxophone
body: The way back in was to stop drawing jazz and look at the place. We pulled the Quebra-Costas steps off Google Maps, from above, and the outline of the staircase turned out to be shaped like a saxophone: a long body curving down into a wide bell where the street opens out.
The real outline was too irregular to be a logo. It was straightened and simplified until it held together at small sizes, without losing the curve that made anyone recognise it in the first place.

Then we went to the place itself, and the visit changed the mark. The staircase stopped being the source of the shape and became the subject of it: the steps are cut out of the saxophone as negative space, so the instrument is made of stairs. Small offsets between the steps keep them from lining up perfectly, which is both how the real staircase is built and the whole point of the music.

chapters.title: Letters cut like steps
chapters.sub: Straight enough to be a building, broken enough to be jazz
body: The wordmark had to belong to the icon rather than sit beside it, so the same cuts went into the letters. QUEBRA JAZZ is heavy and squared off, and every letter is sliced through by a diagonal that takes a piece out of it.

The forms are straight, and that was a decision made against an earlier one. Rounded letters were tried first, for fluidity, and they were wrong: the festival happens on a staircase in a stone city, and the identity wanted the modularity and the structure that goes with that. What keeps it from being rigid is the cuts, which land in different places on every letter and never repeat.
The gaps read two ways depending on how long you look. Blocks stacked and offset, which is the staircase again, and thin bright lines running across a dark field, which is a set of strings.

chapters.title: Two palettes, on purpose
chapters.sub: One for the mark, one for everything shouting outside
body: There is not one set of colours, there are two, and they have different jobs. The mark itself lives in a small, quiet set so it survives everywhere: black, white, and a yellow with a deep purple against it. That pair carries the whole thing on a poster the size of a postcard or on a badge.

Everything shouting for attention in the street gets the second one. Posters and screens run hotter, on oranges, magenta, red and a cyan, because a programme pinned to a wall in Coimbra is competing with a hundred other pieces of paper and the mark is not there to do that work.

The final manual settles the whole thing into five: black, white, a yellow, an orange and a deep purple, each with its values written out in four colour systems so it survives print as well as it survives a screen.

chapters.title: A manual, not a logo
chapters.sub: What happens after the drawing is finished
body: What was handed in is a style guide, and most of it is about the mark surviving contact with the world rather than about how it was drawn.

Two lockups: one stacked, for narrow spaces, and one horizontal, for anything wide like a header. A clear space rule, so nothing crowds it. A negative version for dark grounds. A stated minimum size, which the icon holds down to about eleven millimetres by fourteen. And below that, a simplified icon with the fine detail taken out, because a mark that turns to mud at stamp size needs a version that does not.

The manual also hands the brand over to whoever builds with it next: Gotham Black for headings and Montserrat for text, so the custom lettering of the logo stays special by not being asked to do everything.

chapters.title: It stayed on paper, for now
chapters.sub: The festival does not know it exists
body: The project went well and the teachers liked it. It was an academic exercise from beginning to end: the festival never commissioned it, never saw it, and none of it was ever put out into the world under their name.
That is the part I would like to change. The idea is to take it, one day, to the people who actually run Quebra Jazz, and find out what they make of a stranger having drawn their staircase.

projects.title: NOY, the Noytrall Mascot
projects.contextText: A project developed at jeKnowledge, the UC Junior Enterprise, for a real client brief.
projects.description: Noytrall builds sustainability tech for hotels: guests see the water and energy they use and get rewarded for using less. The product was right and it was cold, so I gave it a face. NOY came out of the company's own logo.

reels.heading: Social & Reels
reels.text: As an extension of the identity, NOY came to life across a series of motion-design reels for Noytrall's social media: more mindful consumption, one stay at a time. Starting with the first one I made.

items.concept: The first reel in the series: NOY's introduction, where the character comes to life for Noytrall's audience.
A Christmas reel: NOY waves and wishes happy holidays. The brand showing up for the season without stepping outside the character's light register.
On awareness and better choices. A simple animation where the app stays in the background. Rather than putting it front and centre it is only glimpsed, so the message lands first.
NOY switches on the air conditioning. Another simple animation, built around a hotel-room gesture, the kind of small choice where sustainability is actually decided.
A walk through the Noytrall app: NOY moves across a few screens, showing the product in motion instead of describing it.

chapters.title: A product with nothing to like
chapters.sub: A real client, and a brand with no face
body: Noytrall is hospitality tech for sustainability. Their product sits in a hotel and shows a guest how much water and electricity their stay is using, then rewards them for bringing it down. It came to jeKnowledge as a real client, and I worked on it there.

The idea is good and the problem was tone. Everything about it was correct, measured and slightly cold: numbers, graphs, a geometric logo. It was asking people to change how they behave in a hotel room, which is a personal thing to ask, and it was asking in the voice of a utility bill.
So the job was not to redesign the brand. It was to give it someone to say it.

chapters.title: The mascot was already in the logo
chapters.sub: I did not invent a character, I found one
body: A mascot bolted onto a brand looks bolted on, so this one had to come from something that was already there. Noytrall's icon is a geometric mark, and its silhouette already had a head in it, with a shape trailing off one side like a tail.

I drew it on paper first, then vectorised it and worked out who NOY was, what it does, what it never does. The result is a character you can put next to the logo without either of them looking borrowed, because one of them is made out of the other.

It is deliberately simple. A round teal head, two eyes, a mouth, and a tail that turns it into a comet when it needs to move. Simple survives being printed small, put on a screen at arm's length, and animated by one person.

chapters.title: Not a drawing, a cast of faces
chapters.sub: A brand has more than one thing to say
body: One pose would have been a logo with eyes. NOY is a set: winking, thinking, delighted, asleep, shocked, disappointed, wearing a hard hat, wearing a crown, holding up a phone, streaking past as a comet, and a Christmas one for December.

That range is the point. A product that congratulates you on Monday, warns you on Tuesday and explains something on Wednesday cannot do all three with the same expression, and a brand that only ever smiles stops being read at all.
They were drawn as stickers, which is also how they get used: dropped into a screen, a post or a story without any layout around them having to change.

chapters.title: Built to hand out the prizes
chapters.sub: Somebody has to do the congratulating
body: The whole product runs on rewarding people for using less, which means the interesting moments are the ones where it says well done. Those are the moments a number cannot carry on its own.

That is what NOY is for. The crown and the medal in the set are not decoration, they are the reward system with a face on it. Being told by a character that you did well is a different feeling from watching a figure change colour, and the difference is the entire reason the mascot exists.

chapters.title: Two dimensions, and a skeleton
chapters.sub: Rigged once, moved many times
body: The obvious route for a mascot that has to move a lot is 3D. This one stayed flat on purpose: the brand is flat, the app is flat, and a 3D character in a 2D product always looks like a visitor.

So the vector illustration was given a rig in After Effects, a set of joints and controls built once, so the same drawing can turn, lean, bounce and gesture without being drawn again. Where the rig is not expressive enough, frames are drawn by hand in Photoshop and dropped in.
That decision is why a series of reels was possible at all. One person cannot animate a character from scratch every week; one person with a rig can.

chapters.title: Where NOY is, and where it cannot be yet
chapters.sub: The social side is out, the product is not
body: The reels below are live, on Noytrall's own social media, and they are the part of this you can go and see. NOY introducing itself, wishing people happy holidays, turning down the air conditioning in a hotel room, walking through the product.

There is more of it than that. NOY runs through the app as well, including the moments nobody thinks of as design, like the screen you look at while something loads and the one that greets you the first time.
The product has not launched, so none of that can be shown here yet. When it does, this page gets the rest of it.

projects.title: Kapout Identity
projects.contextText: An internal project at jeKnowledge, the junior enterprise at the University of Coimbra. No client and no brief.
projects.description: The identity for Kapout, a nightlife app. The mark looks like a Pac-Man and reads as a face that has had one too many: an X for an eye and a bottle where the mouth should be, in neon on black.

mockups.alt: A disc in a pink-to-blue gradient cut through by the silhouette of a bottle, above the Kapout wordmark
mockups.caption: Symbol and wordmark

chapters.title: First it was a beer glass
chapters.sub: I drew the first mark, and the first mark was wrong
body: Before any of this was called Kapout it was called Beer Kapital, and it had a logo to match: a glass of beer, foam on top, the name set inside the glass, in orange and brown.

I drew it, and it was competent and it was a dead end. It was a picture of the thing rather than an idea about the thing, it belonged to one drink at a moment when the product had already stopped being about one drink, and orange and brown are the colours of a pub at four in the afternoon, not of a night out.

One thing from that first page survived everything else. Down in the corner there were five round faces in magenta: sunglasses, smiling, blank, half asleep, and one with two crosses for eyes. Nobody knew it yet, but the last one was the logo.

chapters.title: Flags, moons and an eye
chapters.sub: What got drawn before it landed
body: The next page is a page of attempts. A flag planted on a hill, from the idea of taking ground that the first product notes had in them. A half dome with stars over it. Crescent moons, for the night, in about six versions.

There was a second name in the running as well, Wiseout, with a mark built around an eye. It was drawn far enough to be judged and it lost: it explained itself less immediately and it had none of the humour the product needed.

None of the night imagery worked either, and for the same reason the beer glass had not. A moon says night to everybody and says nothing about this specific thing. What was missing was not a symbol for the night, it was a symbol for what the night does to you.

chapters.title: It is a face, not a Pac-Man
chapters.sub: An X for an eye and a bottle for a mouth
body: The mark is a filled disc with a wedge taken out of it, which is why everybody reads Pac-Man first. Look a second longer and the wedge is a bottle, tipped and pouring, and above it there is a small X where an eye should be.

That X is the whole joke and it came from the very first page. It is the knocked out face from the corner of the beer sketches, promoted to the logo. So the mark is not an arcade reference with a bottle in it, it is a face at the end of the night, and the bottle is the reason it is in that state.

It also assembles itself. There is a four second animation where the bottle flies in and the disc closes around it, so the joke lands in order rather than all at once, which is the version that goes on a screen.

chapters.title: The same head, different nights
chapters.sub: One mark, and a set of moods around it
body: Once the logo is a face it can pull other faces, and a set of them was drawn: sunglasses, hearts for eyes, mouth open in surprise, eyes shut and content, and the two crosses again for the state the app is named after.

They all share one head and one open mouth, so they read as the same character rather than as a bag of emoji. It gives the brand somewhere to go beyond the logo: a reaction on a screen, a sticker in a chat, a state the app can wear when something happens.

chapters.title: Three colours at full volume
chapters.sub: Magenta, purple and cyan, and never on white
body: The palette is short and loud: a magenta, a violet and a cyan, all of them at maximum saturation, over black. Black because the app is used at night and because these three only sing against it. On white they are merely bright; on black they are lit.
The mark takes them in flat versions, one colour at a time, and in a gradient that runs all three across the disc, which is the version that looks most like the inside of a bar.

And there is a deliberately broken one. The logo is duplicated in cyan and magenta and knocked slightly out of register with itself, the way cheap print misaligns and the way a screen looks when your eyes have stopped cooperating. It is the same idea as the X, said with colour instead of drawing.

chapters.title: Prizes cut from the same shape
chapters.sub: The logo, made into something to win
body: The app hands out rewards, and rewards drawn as generic cups would have been a second visual language sitting inside the first one. So the trophies are the mark itself, stood on plinths.

There is a set of them, all illustrated in Illustrator: the disc in different colours of the palette, one carrying the X, one throwing off sparks, one framed by a laurel wreath, one cut as though from crystal. A player collecting them is collecting the logo, over and over, which is the cheapest brand recall there is.

chapters.title: The drawing outlived the product
chapters.sub: It never left the building
body: Kapout stayed internal. It was an idea jeKnowledge had on its own, it never had a client, and it stopped when the people on it were needed on work that mattered more. Nothing here was ever published under the name.

The identity was finished anyway: the mark, its variants, the faces, the palette, the trophies and the animation. It is the piece of the project that still stands up on its own, and it is the reason the whole thing is worth a page.

projects.title: Tabuadela Terraplanagens
projects.contextText: A freelance project produced for an external client.
projects.description: An identity for an earthworks company in Montalegre. The mark is a T that ends in an excavator bucket, and the pine trees of the mountain it works on are held in the gaps between the black shapes.

mockups.alt: A white T monogram, its stem broken into a serrated diagonal, with a half-circle set against its left
mockups.caption: Monogram

chapters.title: A real client with real machines
chapters.sub: Earthworks, demolition and forestry, in Montalegre
body: Tabuadela Terraplanagens prepares the ground that other people build on. Site preparation, demolition, earthmoving, retaining walls, drainage, paving, and forestry work as well. They are based in Montalegre, in the mountains of the north, and they have been going since 2015.

What they asked for was not just a logo. They wanted the brand to look modern and professional, to say versatility without listing sixteen services, to be trusted by a family building a house and by a company hiring a contractor, and to survive being put on a van, a polo shirt, a site banner and a website without falling apart.
So the whole thing was designed against where it would end up rather than against how it would look on a slide.

chapters.title: The first route was the usual one
chapters.sub: And the usual one is this sector's problem
body: The first attempt followed the references the sector already has, and it looked exactly like them: dated, safe, the same as everybody else. That is precisely the thing the company wanted to get away from, so it went in the bin.

The second detour was the opposite mistake. Trying to represent the range of services at once produced marks with arrows, trees and tools stacked into each other, and each one said less than the one before. Trying to say everything is how a mark ends up saying nothing.
The way out was to go back to the five words written at the start and stop adding: machine, force, Montalegre, robustness, versatility.

chapters.title: A bucket, an arm, and a T
chapters.sub: Part of the machine, not the machine
body: The machine had to be in it, but a drawing of a whole excavator is an illustration, not a mark. So only the two parts anybody recognises were kept: the arm and the bucket.

Simplified far enough, those two shapes turn into a T, which is the company's own initial twice over, Tabuadela and Terraplanagens. The vertical of the letter is the arm, the foot of it is the bucket, and the bucket keeps its teeth as a row of serrations along one edge. An orange wedge behind it is the boom, and a half circle at the top is where the cab sits.
It works as a letter for people who never look twice and as a machine for the ones who do, which is the whole job of a monogram in a trade like this.

chapters.title: The pine trees are in what is missing
chapters.sub: Montalegre, held in the gaps
body: The company is not from a generic industrial estate, it is from a specific mountain, and the identity had to carry that without a landscape in it.

It is in the negative space. The gaps cut between the black shapes read as pine trees, the ones that cover the hills the company works on and the forestry side of the business it also lives off. Nobody is required to notice, and the mark loses nothing if they do not.
Everything around it is sharp on purpose. Hard diagonals, high contrast, no rounded corners anywhere. The work is heavy and the mark should not apologise for that.

chapters.title: Black and orange, like the machines
chapters.sub: The colours already on a worksite
body: The palette is two colours: black, and an orange at #F9B233. Neither was chosen from a mood board. They are the colours already on the equipment: black for the weight and the durability of the machines themselves, orange for the parts that exist to be seen, the safety and visibility markings on anything working near people.

The type follows the same logic. A heavy condensed sans, squared and stable, and the name split in two by colour so TABUADELA reads first in orange and TERRAPLANAGENS sits under it in black, which is the order somebody says the company's name out loud.
The T of the wordmark carries the same serrations as the bucket, so the logotype and the icon belong to each other even when they are apart.

chapters.title: Built to go on the side of a van
chapters.sub: Every version the work actually needs
body: A mark for a company like this lives outdoors, at speed, in bad weather, at the wrong angle. So it was delivered as a set rather than a picture.

A horizontal lockup and a stacked one, so it fits a van door and a hard hat. Full colour and white versions, for whatever it is printed on. The icon alone, for anything too small to hold the name. A clear space rule. And a pattern, in black, white and colour, for the surfaces that need to be filled rather than signed.
It was mocked up where it was going to end up: a banner on a building under construction, a container, a work polo, a cap, business cards and letterhead, and the van.

chapters.title: It is out there now
chapters.sub: The best thing a mark can do is get used
body: The client took it, and has recently started putting it to work: it is going up in their advertising and on the things they own.
That is the ending I care about on this one. Every other project on this site was marked, presented or shelved. This one is on a van in Montalegre, doing the job it was drawn for.

projects.title: Cuidados Paliativos, IPO Coimbra
projects.contextText: A freelance project produced for an external client.
projects.description: A visual identity for the palliative care service at IPO Coimbra. The mark is a butterfly that is also a heart, drawn in three translucent colours so that the overlaps make new ones.

chapters.title: Three words, given by the team
chapters.sub: Compassion, respect, dignity
body: The palliative care service at IPO Coimbra looks after people with incurable cancer, and their families and carers. Its work is preventing and relieving suffering, the physical kind and the psychological and spiritual kind, and supporting families through bereavement afterwards.

It is not a service that needs selling, so this was never a brand in the commercial sense. It needed to be recognisable inside a hospital, to feel like the people who work there, and to not look like everything else in a hospital.

The team gave us three words to build on: compassion, respect and dignity. Everything in the identity was measured against those three, alongside research into how palliative care actually works, which is a different thing from how it is imagined.

chapters.title: A butterfly that is also a heart
chapters.sub: Two symbols folded into one shape
body: The butterfly came from the client. It is a symbol the field already uses, for the cycle of life and for transformation, and they wanted it. Drawing only a butterfly would have been doing what was asked and nothing more.

So the icon carries a second thing inside the first. The wings are shaped so that the whole form also reads as a heart, for compassion and for care. Neither reading has to win; most people see one of them and the other one is there when they look again.
It is drawn with soft, fluid curves and nothing sharp anywhere, because the shape is going to be seen by people having the worst week of their lives.
Beside it, Rubik Light. A rounded, open, quiet typeface, chosen for exactly the same reason the curves are curves.

chapters.title: The transparency is the argument
chapters.sub: Where two shapes cross, a third colour appears
body: The parts of the mark are not solid. They are translucent and they lie over each other, and where they cross a new colour appears that belongs to neither of them.

That is the idea, not an effect. Palliative care is three separate parties, the patient, the family and the professionals, and the care itself happens in the places where they overlap. The mark says that without a diagram.

The palette is built to make it work. Three colours carry the identity, a pink, a blue and a lilac, and each of them exists twice: once strong and used at thirty percent opacity, which is what lets the overlaps happen, and once as a solid pale tint for the places where nothing is crossing anything.

chapters.title: One wing, repeated
chapters.sub: A pattern that had to work in black and white too
body: A single stroke was lifted out of the butterfly's wing and set on a grid, turning direction row by row, so the identity has a surface as well as a mark. It fills a folder cover, a lanyard, the back of a card, anywhere the logo would be too much.
The manual shows how it is built, on the grid, so that anybody rebuilding it later gets the same spacing.

And it exists in black and white as well as in colour. That is not a formality in a hospital: a lot of what a service like this prints is photocopied, and a pattern that only works in three translucent colours would have quietly disappeared from half of the things it was made for.

chapters.title: Handed over as a manual
chapters.sub: Rules, so it survives without us
body: What was delivered is a brand manual, because the people who would use this are nurses and doctors and administrative staff, not designers, and the identity had to keep working after we were no longer in the room.

It has a primary logo, a secondary one and a vertical one, so it fits a wide header and a narrow badge. It sets the clear space geometrically, in multiples of a measure taken from the mark itself, rather than as a number that stops making sense when something is scaled. It has black and white versions, the palette written out in four colour systems, the logo shown against each colour of its own palette, and the pattern in its three forms.
The mark was animated as well, so the service has something that moves for a screen. And it was mocked up where it would actually live: an ID card, a lanyard, a mug, a business card.

chapters.title: They loved it, and it was never used
chapters.sub: The honest ending
body: The client liked the concept, and said so. It was never deployed.

There is no better version of that sentence. Work for institutions stops for reasons that have nothing to do with the work, and this one stopped. The manual is finished, the system holds together, and the service still looks the way it looked before.

projects.title: Quebra Jazz Website
projects.contextText: This project was developed for the Web Identity course, part of my Design & Multimedia degree at the University of Coimbra.
projects.description: A site for Quebra Jazz, the free open air jazz festival on the Quebra-Costas steps in Coimbra. Four pages, a shop with a working cart, and a cover where the name of the festival never quite assembles itself.

chapters.title: The brief asked for a wireframe
chapters.sub: We built the site instead
body: The project was a full visual identity for a fictional client, chosen from three options. We took the music festival, and rather than invent one we picked a real one we already knew: Quebra Jazz, the free open air jazz festival held on the Quebra-Costas steps in the old town of Coimbra, the city we study in.

For the website, the brief asked for a wireframe or a prototype in Figma or something like it, showing the main pages. We skipped that step. There was no prototype and no mockup: the design was made straight in the browser, and what got handed in was four working pages in HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

chapters.title: A cover that never settles
chapters.sub: The name is never assembled
body: On the left, QUEBRA runs down the page one letter to a line, stacked like the steps the festival is named after. Floating across it are six pieces of the name, A, EBRA, BRA, RA, ZZ and JAZZ, each sliding from one side to the other on its own clock: five seconds, six, six, four, three and three and a half.

Those numbers share no common beat, so the pieces drift in and out of each other and never come back to the same arrangement twice. The name of the festival is never fully assembled, which is both what the name means and how the music it is named after is played.

Down the right edge there are ten piano keys. Each one slides out from the margin when the pointer touches it and slides back when it leaves. The header is not something you watch, it is something you play.

Below 720 pixels all of it is put away and a plain wordmark takes its place. The pieces need width to drift across and a phone has none, and an animation squeezed into a space it does not fit is worse than no animation at all.

chapters.title: Four pages, one base
chapters.sub: And a free typeface doing a paid one's job
body: The site is a home page, a shop, a sign up page and a contact page. Every one of them loads the same base stylesheet first, where the colours, the type and the spacing live as variables, so the shop and the form could not quietly drift away from each other as they grew.

Everything that appears on scroll is marked in the markup and watched by a single observer, so there is one answer to the question of when a block may arrive rather than one answer per page. Where the browser is set to reduce motion, it stops.

The style guide asks for Gotham Black in headings. Gotham is a paid family and we did not have it, so the site sets its headings in Anton with Montserrat underneath: the same flat, heavy, blocky weight, for nothing.

The home page also carries the things a festival site has to carry. The programme, eight nights with their dates and their names, a block of figures from the previous edition, and a map of the street the whole thing happens on.

chapters.title: A shop that actually works
chapters.sub: Twenty four products and a cart that remembers
body: The shop holds twenty four products across four categories, with a category bar that sticks to the top and lights up whichever section you have scrolled into.

Some products carry their own variants in the markup, so choosing black or white, or a men's or women's cut, swaps the photograph without leaving the grid. Clicking a product opens it larger, in a panel over the page.

The cart is not a picture of a cart. It keeps its contents in the browser's own storage, so they are still there after a reload, opens as a drawer from the side, and answers every time you add something: the counter jumps, and a small message says what went in and offers to show you.

chapters.title: Putting a band forward, in four steps
chapters.sub: A long form that does not feel long
body: Bands apply to play through a form with a lot of questions in it. Asked all at once it is the kind of page people close, so it is cut into four steps, the band, the criteria, the performance and the last details, with a bar across the top showing how far along you are.

Each step is checked before it lets you move on, so a mistake is caught where it was made instead of at the end. Sending is simulated, since nothing here has anywhere to be sent: the form is replaced by a confirmation.
Behind it, three photographs of the festival cross fade into each other every six seconds, slowly enough to be scenery rather than something competing for attention with the questions.

chapters.title: The teachers liked it
chapters.sub: Because it was a site and not a drawing of one
body: It went very well. The site was the part of the project that stood out, and the teachers liked it.

What made the difference was not the code, it was the difference between describing a thing and handing it over. The brief asked for a picture of a website, and what arrived was a website: pages you move through, a cart that remembers, a form that answers back.
Everything stayed a concept. The festival is real, but the identity and this site were never commissioned and never ran for it.

projects.title: Kapout App
projects.contextText: An internal project at jeKnowledge, the junior enterprise at the University of Coimbra. No client and no brief.
projects.description: A nightlife app that turns a night out with friends into something you play: drinks counted, challenges taken on, and a leaderboard running between the group until morning.

chapters.title: Nobody asked for this
chapters.sub: No client, no brief
body: Kapout was not a commission. It started inside jeKnowledge, the junior enterprise at the University of Coimbra, as an idea the team wanted to try out, half a challenge and half a game to see what would come of it. It was one of the first things I worked on there as a trainee.

That meant there was no brief to answer and nobody to please, which sounds easier than it is. With nothing fixed, the only thing holding the project up was whether the idea was any good, so the first real work was deciding what a night out actually needs from an app.

chapters.title: A night out, as a game
chapters.sub: Points, challenges and ground to take
body: The app counts what a group drinks across the night, but counting on its own is a spreadsheet. The point was to make the night something you play together: a leaderboard running between friends, challenges to take on, and shots and other drinks worth different things.

The first page of notes is all of that and nothing else. A board, challenges, drinks, and a flag planted in ground you have taken. A night out already works a bit like that without anyone saying so, and the app just kept score.

It is built around the group rather than around one person. Alone, a drink counter is a health app, and a fairly sad one. With four friends around a table the same number stops being a measurement and becomes a result.

chapters.title: When the name stopped fitting
chapters.sub: It started out as Beer Kapital
body: The project's first name was Beer Kapital, and for the first version of the idea it fitted: beer, a board, ground to take.

The app kept growing, though, and beer stopped being the whole of it. Shots, challenges, everything a group puts each other through over a night. A name that mentioned one drink was going to end up smaller than the thing it was sitting on.

So it became Kapout. It is short, it is easy to shout across a bar, and it carries three things at once: cap out, going as far as you can go; go out; and that's cap, the slang for a story nobody believes, which is most of what gets told the next morning about the night before.

chapters.title: Designed to be used in the dark
chapters.sub: Neon on black, and prizes worth winning
body: Everything about the interface comes from where it gets used. A dark room, noise, the phone held at arm's length and nobody reading carefully. So the screens are close to black with a small set of colours turned all the way up, magenta, purple and cyan, and the things you press are large and few.

The rewards are drawn rather than listed. I illustrated a set of trophies in Illustrator, all built out of the same shape as the brand mark, so that winning something looks like winning something instead of a line appearing in a table.
The whole product was designed in Figma. Madalena Conceição joined later and built out some of the app's screens there with me.

chapters.title: It stayed a prototype
chapters.sub: Stopped by work that mattered more
body: Kapout never left prototyping. The team took it as far as turning the design into a coded prototype, and then it stopped. Other projects mattered more and the people were needed on them.

That is the ordinary end of an idea a company has on its own, and it is worth saying plainly rather than dressing it up. What the project gave me was all of it, from the name to the last screen, at a point where I had only just started.

projects.title: EatEasy
projects.contextText: This project was developed for the Information Systems course, part of my Design & Multimedia degree at the University of Coimbra.
projects.description: A web platform for finding and booking restaurants, with two sides to it: the people booking a table, and the people who own the place. Built in PHP over a PostgreSQL database, and still online.

mockups.alt: The dish illustrations used across the EatEasy interface
mockups.caption: Illustrations used in the interface

chapters.title: Two different people, one site
chapters.sub: Whoever books, and whoever takes the booking
body: EatEasy was the project for the Information Systems course, made with Carolina Seixas. The idea was a platform for booking restaurants that had to serve two people with opposite jobs at the same time.

One of them wants to find somewhere to eat: search by city or by kind of food, look at a place, book a table, and later say what it was like. The other one owns the restaurant: put the venue on the platform, keep its information up to date, and accept or turn down the bookings that come in.
They are not the same site with a different button. They are two front doors, each with its own home page and its own profile, and almost everything behind them is different.

chapters.title: Drawn first, coded after
chapters.sub: Everything went through Figma
body: None of the interface was invented in the editor. The whole thing was prototyped and designed in Figma first, both flows, screen by screen, and only then written as code. The reports we handed in carry those prototypes next to the navigation diagram, which is how the two halves stayed in step.

The look is one deep teal with a lighter one over it, Inter throughout, generous corners and soft shadows. It is quiet on purpose: the screen is mostly photographs of food and lists of places, and the interface's job is to not compete with them.

chapters.title: No filler data
chapters.sub: Around twenty restaurants, all properly filled in
body: Nothing on the platform says Lorem Ipsum or Restaurant 1. It runs on a made-up but complete set of around twenty restaurants, each with a real-looking name, a city, one or more kinds of cuisine, an average price, a phone number, an email and a rating.

That is what makes the rest testable. Searching, filtering by cuisine and filtering by date only mean something against a set big enough to return different answers, and a list of placeholders would have hidden every problem worth finding.
On top of that sit the things a client does over time: favourites, bookings that can be cancelled, and ratings with comments left after the visit.

chapters.title: The database never forgets
chapters.sub: Every change keeps its old value
body: Editing a profile or a restaurant does not just overwrite what was there. Before writing, the code reads the row as it stands and, for every field that actually changed, stores the old value with the date it stopped being true.
The state of every booking is kept the same way, so the path from requested to accepted or refused stays on record instead of collapsing into whatever it says today.
It costs a table and a loop, and it turns the database from a picture of the present into a record of what happened. It is the part of this project I would build the same way again.

chapters.title: Charts for whoever owns the place
chapters.sub: The data read back to its owner
body: The owner's side is not only a list of bookings to approve. The platform reads its own database and gives it back as charts, so the person running a restaurant can see how many bookings came in, how they are distributed and how the place is doing over time.
It is the same information the client side hides on purpose. A visitor wants one table on one night; an owner wants the shape of a month.

chapters.title: Still online
chapters.sub: It went well, and it did not stop at the mark
body: The project was well received and the teacher liked it. The two of us wrote it together over 149 commits on GitLab, with Carolina doing more of the database and me more of the design and the front end.

The part I am most pleased with is that it did not stop when the course did. It is packaged in a container running PHP and Apache, the database moved to Postgres hosted on Neon, and the whole thing is deployed and open to anybody with the link, which is not where most coursework ends up.

projects.title: Abrigo
projects.partners: Afonso Almeida · Pedro Teixeira · Tiago Gomes
projects.contextText: This project was developed for the Interactive Media Design course, part of my Design & Multimedia degree at the University of Coimbra.
projects.description: An emergency app for civilians during a war, made for a phone with almost no signal, almost no battery and somebody frightened holding it. Shelters, a kit that keeps itself up to date, and a way to call for help in one movement.

mockups.alt: The Abrigo mark: a house whose negative space forms a human figure, above the ABR!GO wordmark
mockups.caption: Symbol and wordmark

chapters.title: Design for the worst day
chapters.sub: One disaster, chosen and stuck to
body: The brief was to design an interactive artefact that helps people before, during or after a disaster, and to pick one kind and stay with it. We chose war.

It brings its own rules with it, and they are the opposite of the ones an app is usually built under. No internet worth relying on. Possibly no power. Infrastructure that may already be broken. And a person using it who is frightened, in a hurry, and not going to read anything carefully.
So the target was never a beautiful app. It was one that still works on the worst day of somebody's life.

chapters.title: Five people, five different emergencies
chapters.sub: The same app, needed for opposite reasons
body: Before drawing a single screen we wrote who this was for, and it was not one person. A young man walking home who needs to know which streets to avoid. A mother on shift at a hospital whose first thought is the school her children are in. A civil first responder who gets an alert that somebody near him needs help. A preparer who keeps an emergency kit and wants it checked. An elderly man, alone, who suddenly cannot breathe.

Each of them got a scenario written as a story, from the ordinary moment before, through the alert, to how it ends. Those stories are what set the app's parts: a live map with the areas to avoid and safer routes, shelters, an inventory that warns you when the food and medicine are close to expiring, a way to reach people, and a call for help that goes out with your location and your medical details attached.
The last one is the one that decided the design. If Alberto can only manage a single movement, then everything else on this app has to be arranged around that movement being possible.

chapters.title: Broken on paper first
chapters.sub: Wizard of Oz, before anything was real
body: Nothing was made in high fidelity until the idea had been through people. We tested on paper, with a Wizard of Oz set-up: the person holds the sketch and acts, and one of us plays the part of the app, changing the screen by hand as they go.

It is a cheap way to be told you are wrong. The button to call for help was pressed by mistake over and over, by people who thought it meant general help with using the app. Others went to the emergency kit looking for their own profile. The tips page was read as tips on how to use the app rather than as what to do in an emergency.

All three got fixed there and then. Asking for help became a slider instead of a button, so it cannot happen by accident, and it stopped being called Ask For Help and became SOS. Being told this on paper cost an afternoon. Being told it after the interface was built would have cost the interface.

chapters.title: We built the thing that tested it
chapters.sub: Not a form, an instrument
body: For the real usability testing we did not want a questionnaire someone fills in afterwards from memory, so we built our own site to run the sessions.

It takes the participant through the whole protocol. An intake questionnaire and a consent step first. Then the tasks, one at a time, each of them timed by the site itself, with the person rating how hard it was as soon as they finish it. Then a closing questionnaire about the language, the colours, the type and whether they could see themselves using it under stress. Everything lands in one place, and there is an administrator area that reads it all back as charts.
It is the difference between remembering that a task felt slow and knowing how long it took. That is the site below, still running.

chapters.title: Black, and one yellow
chapters.sub: The colour of a warning sign
body: The interface is black with a single yellow on it.
