Black because a screen that is mostly dark asks the least of a battery and of a pair of eyes at night, and the yellow for the contrast against it and because it is the colour this kind of information already has in the world, on the signs that mark caution and danger.

Everything else is about a hand that is not steady. Large targets, high contrast, the fewest steps a critical action can be done in, and type on the Material Design 3 scale, which we then audited the interface against rather than only borrowing from.
The full high-fidelity design lives in Figma, and the prototype below is the one we presented.

chapters.title: And then it was built
chapters.sub: Not a click-through, a set of pages
body: The prototype did not stop in Figma. The core of the app was written as real pages, so the screens that matter can be opened on a phone and used with a thumb instead of clicked through in a viewer.

It is the home, the map, the emergency kit, the messages and the tips page, sharing one stylesheet with the palette and the type scale in it. Opening it on an actual phone is the only way to find out whether the targets really are big enough, and no viewer will tell you that.

chapters.title: Top marks, and a name they liked
chapters.sub: The process was the point, and it showed
body: The project got the top mark. The teacher liked the name, and at the end of the presentation we were congratulated for the work.

What was being marked was never only the app. The course was about going through every step of an interaction design process properly, and this is the project where we argued the most, went back the most times, and threw away the most. That is the reason the last version is the one it is.

projects.title: Capicua, Lenga
projects.contextText: This project was developed for the Audiovisual Production course, part of my Design & Multimedia degree at the University of Coimbra.
projects.description: An animated music video for Lenga, by the Portuguese artist Capicua. Every frame drawn one at a time, in the register of a child's drawing, with a girl walking through the places the lyrics name.

chapters.title: Taking the lyrics at their word
chapters.sub: A school, a history book, a mountain
body: The exercise was a music video and we had to pick a song from a list. We settled on Capicua first, as the artist, and then went looking through her for the right one. Lenga won because of what it is about: childhood, school, the things you are taught. Carolina loved the lyrics, I came round to them, and that was that.
We pulled lines out of the song and built the places they name. A school. A history book. A mountain range. Nothing is a metaphor for the line, it is the line, drawn.

It is literal and symbolic at the same time, and that is the trick of it: a viewer follows the images without needing to decode anything, and the meaning arrives through the song rather than through the picture explaining itself.

chapters.title: A girl who says nothing
chapters.sub: The thread between the places
body: A set of illustrated places is a slideshow. What makes it a film is a person moving through them, so a main character was added: a child who crosses each space and connects them into one small journey.

She never speaks and nothing on screen explains her. Everything she is comes from the body: how she stands, how she moves, how fast she goes. It is the oldest way to carry a narrative and it is the one that does not compete with a song already full of words.

She is wearing headphones in almost every scene, which is the small thing that ties the whole video together. She is listening to the song we are listening to, and the places she walks through are what it is putting in her head.

chapters.title: Drawn the way a child draws
chapters.sub: Simple line, soft shapes, lettering by hand
body: The visual register comes from children's drawings. A simple, unfussy outline, soft organic shapes, and lettering done by hand rather than typed. The words on screen are few, the title and little else: the song is doing the talking and putting its lyrics up as well would have been saying everything twice.

That is not a shortcut, it is a match. The song is about childhood and about the things you are told when you are small, and a slick, corrected, perfectly aligned video would have argued with it. The imperfection is the argument.

chapters.title: Every frame drawn once
chapters.sub: No copying, no interpolation
body: The animation is frame by frame, and the rule we set was that no drawing gets reused. Every frame is its own drawing, made from scratch, across every scene in the film.

It is a brutal way to work and it buys one specific thing. Because no two frames were drawn identically, the line never sits still: it shifts and wobbles very slightly from frame to frame, which is the texture people recognise from hand-drawn animation and which no software will fake convincingly.
It also enforces a discipline. When every frame costs the same amount of work, you stop animating things that do not need to move, and the film gets tighter as a result.

chapters.title: A minute and a half that keeps moving
chapters.sub: The drawing never quite settles
body: The finished video runs a minute and twenty-eight seconds, and there is not a still moment in it, even where nothing is happening. The line itself is always breathing.
For a minute and a half of film it is a great deal of drawing, and the reason for doing it that way is visible in every second of it.

chapters.title: Made two-handed
chapters.sub: One song, split down the middle
body: It went well, and again the mark is not the interesting part. This was a good project to be inside: one song, one rule, and a colleague to argue with about what a verse looks like.

The problems it threw up were the enjoyable kind. How many drawings a walk needs before it stops reading as a stutter. How to keep a face recognisable when you have redrawn it from nothing over and over. Where to let the line go loose, because the song is loose in that bar too.
Carolina and I worked on all of it together rather than dividing it into halves, which for something drawn frame by frame is the only way it gets finished at all.

projects.title: A Última Chama
projects.contextText: This project was developed for the Audiovisual Production course, part of my Design & Multimedia degree at the University of Coimbra.
projects.description: A stop-motion short taken from the Apocalypse of Lorvão, an illuminated manuscript from 1189. A knight and a dragon fight it out on the manuscript's own pages, in paper cut-outs photographed one frame at a time.

chapters.title: The book is the set
chapters.sub: The film happens on the page, not in a place
body: The exercise handed us a book to work from: the Apocalypse of Lorvão, an illuminated manuscript made at the Lorvão monastery in 1189 and now held in the national archive.

We took it very literally, which was the decision the whole film came out of. Rather than adapting the story into a world of its own, the film stays inside the book. The pages under the animation are the manuscript's own, so the fight is happening on the actual object it came from.

It settles everything else at once. If the stage is a page, the animation has to be flat and made of paper, the camera has to look straight down, and the whole thing has to look handmade, because the thing it is imitating was made by hand eight hundred years ago.

chapters.title: A knight and a dragon, taken from the illuminations
chapters.sub: The oldest story there is, on purpose
body: The story is good against evil, and there was no attempt to complicate it. Good is a knight on a horse. Evil is a dragon that breathes fire. Anybody can follow it with the sound off.

What makes it belong to the source is where the characters come from. Both were drawn out of the manuscript's own illuminations, so the proportions, the postures and the strangeness are the medieval ones and not ours. Everything was then drawn and painted by hand, characters and backgrounds alike.
Drawing them ourselves rather than cutting up the scans matters: the manuscript is a reference, not a texture to borrow.

chapters.title: One photograph at a time
chapters.sub: Paper, moved by hand, shot from above
body: The animation is stop motion, and the whole rig was a phone camera held over the table by something we put together ourselves. The pieces are paper, they get moved a few millimetres, and they get photographed, over and over, and the film is what those photographs become when they are played in order.
It was shot in separate scenes and assembled afterwards: the castle, the knight riding, the sword coming out, the dragon turning, and the fight. Between them they come to several hundred photographs.

The method is slow and it is also the reason the film looks the way it does. Paper photographed under a light has a texture and a slight unsteadiness that nothing generated afterwards can imitate, and that unsteadiness is exactly what a hand-painted manuscript already has.

chapters.title: Half of it is sound
chapters.sub: A silent stop motion of paper is just paper
body: Cut-outs sliding across a page do not read as a fight. What turns them into one is what you hear: hooves, a blade leaving its scabbard, fire, impact, and the pause before each of them.

The track is a mix. A good deal of it is library material, chosen and cut to the action, and some of it we recorded ourselves. The fire is the one that stuck. Either way, all of it then has to be lined up frame by frame against the picture, which is where most of the work in a sequence like this actually goes.
It is also what carries the drama. The animation is deliberately simple; the sound is what makes a simple drawing feel like it weighs something.

chapters.title: Assembling it, and putting the words in
chapters.sub: Where the pieces become a film
body: The edit is where the photographs stop being folders and become a minute and forty-seven seconds. Sequences joined, timings adjusted, and the colour steadied so the light holds from one scene to the next.
The typography was added here rather than drawn into the frames, so the words sit on the film the way text sits on a manuscript page, and the credits close it.

chapters.title: Two of us and a table
chapters.sub: The problems were the good part
body: It went well, and the grade is not the part worth writing down. What I keep from it is that this was a genuinely good thing to make: the two of us, a table, a pile of cut paper and a phone held above it.

Every scene came with a problem that only exists in this way of working. How far a wing travels between two photographs before the flap reads as a flap. How to keep a horse looking like it is running when it is a flat shape being nudged by a finger. How loud a fire has to be before a paper dragon starts to look dangerous.

None of that can be planned in advance and all of it is the enjoyable part. Carolina and I split everything down the middle, from the drawing to the shooting to the sound, and the film is the two of us the whole way through.

projects.title: O Sonho (Zobeide)
projects.contextText: This project was developed for the Project II course, part of my Design & Multimedia degree at the University of Coimbra.
projects.description: A short film built out of Zobeide, one of Italo Calvino's invisible cities. Five strangers dream the same woman on the same foggy street, and spend their lives chasing her. No dialogue, six minutes, shot at night in Coimbra.

chapters.title: I picked a city that does not exist
chapters.sub: Zobeide, out of Calvino
body: The brief started from Italo Calvino's Invisible Cities, and each of us chose one to work from. I took Zobeide, and the reasons were written down before anything was shot.
The first was the subject. Zobeide is about desire and obsession, about chasing something that is never caught, which is a thing everybody recognises whether or not they have read the book.

The second was colder and just as important. Zobeide is a city of repeating streets and closed spaces, which means it can be built with almost nothing. A student film that needs a spectacle is a student film that fails, and this one could be carried by symbol and mood instead.

chapters.title: Five men and the same dream
chapters.sub: A mason, a navigator, an architect, a visionary, a cartographer
body: Five men who have never met dream the same thing on the same night: narrow streets under fog, and the silhouette of a woman who turns a corner and is gone before they reach her.

They wake up with the dream still sharp, and each one goes looking for it. Their paths cross, and together they set about making the place from the dream real. Time passes, what they have built grows, and so does the doubt about whether any of it was ever worth it.
Then a woman walks into it, carrying a suitcase, and nobody knows who she is. That is the end, and it is where the film finally lets the tension go.
Each man has a trade and a room of his own, and the film introduces them the same way: a corridor, a bed, a small gesture. Taking off shoes. Taking off glasses. Blowing out a candle.

chapters.title: Not one word is spoken
chapters.sub: The sound was written before the picture
body: There is no dialogue anywhere in the film, and that was decided at the start rather than arrived at by accident. The story is about something nobody can explain, including to themselves, so letting the characters explain it would have undone it.

What replaces dialogue is a sound list that existed before we shot a frame: footsteps that repeat until they turn into a loop, a clock, blankets, the calm breathing of someone asleep and the ragged breathing of someone waking badly, drunk voices somewhere out in the street, wind.
The sound was the part I took on most of, and in a film with nothing being said it is not accompaniment, it is where half the meaning lives.

chapters.title: Coimbra at night, lit by a car
chapters.sub: Borrowed clothes, real fog, four nights
body: It was shot in Coimbra, in the streets of the city, and in the houses of people we know, because a film with five men who each need a bedroom needs five bedrooms and no budget for a set.
The costume is period, late nineteenth into the twentieth century, and it came from the local folk dance group, who lent it to us. The actors are colleagues of ours.

The light was a car. We used the headlights, pointed where the shot needed them, which is the sort of solution that is only embarrassing until you see it on screen. And the fog, which the whole dream depends on, is not a machine and is not an effect: it is the actual night mist that Coimbra has anyway, and we shot on the nights it was there.
Four nights of filming and something close to five hundred takes, in 4K, for six minutes of finished film.

chapters.title: The labyrinth is in the edit
chapters.sub: We never built a city
body: The story has them raising a city out of their dream. We did not build one, and we never intended to. That is the gap every adaptation has to solve and it is the part of the project I am most pleased with.

The labyrinth is made in the cutting room. Actors walking and running through real streets, shot from angles that hide where they are, cut so that they seem to pass the same corner more than once and to arrive where they started. Close shots for how alone each man is, wide ones for how big the thing is that they are inside of.
The audience is given the feeling of a labyrinth instead of the sight of one, and a feeling is cheaper and lasts longer.

chapters.title: The one that went best
chapters.sub: And the thanks it is owed
body: Of everything I made at university, this is the project that was received best. I am not going to put the mark on a website, but it was the top of anything I have done.

It is also the most conceptual thing here. There is no dialogue, no explanation and nothing in it that tells you what to feel, and it asks the person watching to meet it somewhere. That was the risk of it and it is the reason it worked.

It was made with Ana Oliveira and Rafael Campos, and it does not exist without the five actors who gave it their nights. The delivery also included a moving poster and a set of teasers, cut from the same material.

projects.title: Silvestre, Opening Titles
projects.contextText: This project was developed for the Typography in Digital Media course, part of my Design & Multimedia degree at the University of Coimbra.
projects.description: An original opening-title sequence for Silvestre, João César Monteiro's 1982 film. Shot on a bedroom table with a candle held against the objects, and screened in cinemas during the Caminhos do Cinema Português festival.

chapters.title: The film was handed to me
chapters.sub: Silvestre, and no say in it
body: The exercise was to make opening titles for a Portuguese film, and the films were assigned off a list. Mine was Silvestre, by João César Monteiro, from 1982.

The whole thing existed because of the festival. Caminhos do Cinema Português, the only festival in the country given entirely to Portuguese film, was reaching its thirtieth edition and giving an award to the actor Luís Miguel Cintra, so every film on the list was one he is in.

First thing I did was watch it. It would have been possible to work from a synopsis and it would have been the wrong way round: the brief was to set the tone of a film from its first frame, and you cannot set a tone you have not sat through.

chapters.title: A pair of scissors tells the whole film
chapters.sub: Objects instead of illustration
body: The sequence is made of things, filmed close. Not drawings of things and not stock footage of things: real objects, arranged on a table and shot at macro distance so that they fill the frame and stop being ordinary.

The one that carries it is a pair of scissors, which in the film is what the woman uses to cut off her hair so she can pass as a man. Put on a table on its own, in the dark, an ordinary household object turns into an instrument, and the audience has been told what kind of film this is before a single title card has finished.
That is the whole method: pick the objects the story turns on, and let the lighting make them ominous.

chapters.title: A candle held against the objects
chapters.sub: A bedroom, a table, and one flame
body: There was no studio and no lighting kit. It was shot at home, on a table, with a phone, and the only light is a candle held close to whatever is being filmed.

That is not a limitation being made the best of, it is the reason the sequence looks the way it does. A flame is never still, so the shadows move on their own the entire time, and everything in the frame sits in hard chiaroscuro with a warm edge. It gives the whole thing a phantasmagoric quality that steady lighting cannot produce and that no filter imitates convincingly.
The warmth also does a second job. It puts the images in the past without a single caption saying so.

chapters.title: Baskerville, because of when it is set
chapters.sub: And credits cut to the sound
body: The typeface is Baskerville, chosen for its formality and its age. It is a face with history in it, and setting the credits in it ties the sequence to the period the story lives in, quietly, without anybody having to notice why.

The brief fixed what had to appear: the title, the director, the producer, the director of photography, four actors including Luís Miguel Cintra, the year, and my own name under titles design. Working inside a fixed list of credits is the typographic exercise.

The titles are cut to the sound rather than laid over it. Each one arrives on a sharp fade with an effect landing at the same instant, which turns what would have been a text roll into something with a pulse.

chapters.title: It was shown in a cinema
chapters.sub: And who helped make it
body: The best sequences from the exercise were selected to be projected during the festival, and mine was one of them. It was shown at the TAGV and at Casa do Cinema, and I went to see it.
That is a different thing from a mark. A title sequence is made to run in the dark in front of people, and this one got to do that.
It was made alone, start to finish, except for a few things in front of the camera that I needed a second pair of hands for. My mother and my brother, who deserve the credit for it.

projects.title: Sísifo
projects.contextText: This project was developed for the Computer Graphics course, part of my Design & Multimedia degree at the University of Coimbra.
projects.description: A twelve second 3D animation built around a constraint: the brief handed over a ball already animated to spin, and a camera that could not move. A beetle was put behind it to give the spinning a reason.

mockups.alt: The 3D beetle pushing its ball, seen from three-quarters behind
mockups.caption: 3D model, rear view

chapters.title: They gave me a ball that spins
chapters.sub: And a camera I was not allowed to move
body: The exercise did not start from a blank file. It came with a ball whose rotation was already animated and not to be touched, a camera under restrictions, a base scene, and ten seconds to do something with all of it.
That is a stranger problem than it sounds. A ball turning on the spot is not a shot, it is a fact with no cause. Everything I built exists to answer one question: why is that thing spinning?

chapters.title: I threw the office out
chapters.sub: A forest instead of a desk
body: The base scene we were handed was an office interior. I did not use it. I deleted it and built somewhere else entirely, outdoors, with a mountain behind and a forest floor in front.

That was more work than accepting the room, and it was the decision the whole film depended on. A ball rolling across an office carpet has nowhere to go and nothing to mean. A ball on the ground in a forest has both.

chapters.title: The beetle is the reason the ball turns
chapters.sub: Sisyphus, with six legs
body: The answer was to put an animal behind it. A beetle pushing a ball of matter is a thing that exists, everybody has seen one, and it explains the rotation completely without a word of setup.

It also brought the title. A creature pushing a weight uphill forever is the myth of Sisyphus, and once the beetle was in the scene the whole thing stopped being an exercise with a ball in it and became a very small film about a task that does not end.
It is the one thing in the scene modelled from nothing: body, legs and shell, built in Blender specifically for this.

chapters.title: What is mine and what I fetched
chapters.sub: Detail at the front, tricks at the back
body: Beyond the beetle, the scene is assembled rather than sculpted, and that is deliberate. Some of the vegetation is carried over from my own earlier projects. The rest, trees and rocks, came from BlenderKit and Sketchfab, and the textures from libraries like AmbientCG and PolyHaven.

What decides quality in a build like this is not how much was modelled but where the effort went. Only the objects near the camera are properly modelled with clean, optimised meshes. The trees in the far background are fakes, simplified until they cost almost nothing, because nobody looks at them and the render has to finish.

The main elements carry full texture sets, albedo, normal and displacement, applied with UV mapping and touched up in Photoshop where the seams showed. The lighting is a sun for the shadows plus an ambient HDRI at a controlled intensity for the soft fill, with the shadows tuned to keep the foreground, the forest and the mountain reading as three separate distances.

chapters.title: The legs, and the bird that ends it
chapters.sub: A walk cycle locked to somebody else's rotation
body: The beetle walks on a full push-loop cycle, with overlapping action through the legs so they do not move as one piece, and the whole cycle is locked to the speed the ball was already turning at. The animation I made has to agree with the animation I was given, exactly, or the illusion collapses.

Then a bird comes in and takes the beetle. Its wing animation was imported and modified to loop cleanly; what I built is the path it flies, drawn by hand with Bézier curves and keyframes in the NLA editor, with slow in and out so the arc reads as a body with weight rather than a shape sliding across the frame.
It arrives in the last seconds and it is the joke. The beetle finally stops pushing, but not the way it wanted to.

chapters.title: Twelve seconds, and a punchline
chapters.sub: The sound came last
body: Sound went on afterwards, in post. Some of it I recorded myself, the rest came from a library, and it is what turns a clean render into somewhere with air in it.

The finished thing runs twelve seconds. Everything above, the scene, the animal, the walk cycle, the textures, exists to fill them, and the whole point was to get a small complete story inside them without breaking one rule the brief set: the camera stayed where it was told, and the ball turns exactly as it was handed to me.
